questions.stem: By 1914, which two African states remained free of European colonial rule?
options: Ghana and Nigeria
Sudan and Somalia
Ethiopia and Liberia
Egypt and Morocco
questions.explanation: After the Scramble for Africa, only Ethiopia, which defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896, and Liberia stayed independent. Egypt was under British control and Morocco became a French protectorate in 1912.

questions.stem: British officials in Nigeria under Frederick Lugard governed through existing chiefs and emirs. This system is known as:
options: the mandate system
indirect rule
assimilation
apartheid
questions.explanation: Indirect rule kept traditional rulers in place under British supervision, which was cheaper and needed fewer officials. France officially aimed at assimilation, turning colonial elites into French citizens in culture.

questions.stem: Which belief was most often used in the early 20th century to justify colonial rule?
options: That colonised peoples had voted in referendums to join the European empires
That Europeans had a duty to 'civilise' peoples judged unready to govern themselves
That colonies would be given independence once they had repaid the cost of conquest
That international law required powerful states to govern their weaker neighbours
questions.explanation: Ideas such as the 'civilising mission' and the 'white man's burden', often backed by Social Darwinism, presented empire as a moral duty. They masked economic and strategic motives and denied colonised peoples' capacity to govern themselves.

questions.stem: The Indian National Congress, which led the main campaign for Indian independence, was founded in:
questions.explanation: Congress began in 1885 as a moderate body of educated Indians seeking a greater voice in government. The All-India Muslim League was founded in 1906.

questions.stem: The Pan-African Congress held in Manchester in 1945 is significant because:
options: European powers agreed there on a timetable for granting independence to every colony
it was the first meeting at which Africans voted to join the British Commonwealth
future leaders such as Nkrumah and Kenyatta attended and demanded independence for Africa
it created the Organisation of African Unity and drew up its founding charter for the continent
questions.explanation: The fifth Pan-African Congress, with W.E.B. Du Bois present, moved from asking for reform to demanding independence. Kwame Nkrumah and Jomo Kenyatta later led their countries to independence. The OAU was founded in 1963.

questions.stem: The Amritsar massacre of April 1919, when troops under General Dyer fired on an unarmed crowd, affected the Indian nationalist movement mainly by:
options: leading Britain to promise India full independence within the following year
causing the Muslim League to break away from Congress for the first time
turning many moderates, including Gandhi, against continued British rule
persuading Congress to give up protest and accept British rule for a decade
questions.explanation: The killing of hundreds in the Jallianwala Bagh, and the praise some Britons gave Dyer, shattered faith in British justice. Gandhi launched the non-cooperation movement in 1920. The Muslim League had been separate since 1906.

questions.stem: How did the First World War encourage movements for self-determination in the colonies?
options: The peace treaties granted full independence to all the colonies of the defeated Central Powers
Britain and France promised in 1918 to give their colonies independence within ten years
The war ended the economic value of the colonies, so empires began to give them up
Colonial troops served abroad, and Wilson's ideals raised hopes that empires then ignored
questions.explanation: More than a million Indians served overseas, and Wilson's Fourteen Points spread the language of self-determination. But at Paris it was applied mainly in Europe; German and Ottoman lands became League mandates under Britain and France, which bred disillusion.

questions.stem: Article 22 of the League of Nations Covenant described the well-being of peoples in former enemy colonies as 'a sacred trust of civilisation'. Which statement best evaluates the mandate system that followed?
options: It placed every colony in the world under League supervision, including those of Britain and France
It accepted that colonial rule should answer to an international body, but in practice extended empire
It gave immediate independence to the former German colonies in Africa and the Pacific under League law
It ended imperial rule in the Middle East, since all the mandates became independent before the 1930s
questions.explanation: Mandatory powers reported to the Permanent Mandates Commission, an early idea of international accountability. Yet Britain, France, Australia and others governed the territories much like colonies. Iraq, a mandate, gained independence in 1932, but most did not until after 1945.

questions.stem: In the Atlantic Charter of August 1941, Roosevelt and Churchill declared the right of all peoples to choose their form of government. Why did this matter for colonial nationalists?
options: It committed Britain to granting independence to India and Burma as soon as the war ended
It set up the UN Trusteeship Council to supervise all of the colonies in Asia and Africa after 1945
It was signed by the leaders of Congress and the Muslim League as well as by Churchill and FDR
They used it to claim self-determination, though Churchill said it applied to Nazi-occupied Europe
questions.explanation: Nationalists in Asia and Africa quoted the Charter's third principle, and the USA was openly critical of empire. Churchill told the Commons in September 1941 that it was aimed at restoring nations under Nazi rule, not at the British Empire.

questions.stem: Historians often call the fall of Singapore in February 1942 a turning point for European empires in Asia. Which reason best supports this view?
options: Britain responded by giving Malaya and Singapore independence in the same year
The defeat forced the USA to take over Britain's Asian colonies for the rest of the war
Japan's victories destroyed the myth that European rule could not be challenged
Japan granted full independence to Singapore and Malaya immediately after victory
questions.explanation: The rapid defeat of British, Dutch, French and American forces in 1941-1942 shattered European prestige. In places such as Indonesia and Burma the Japanese also sponsored nationalist leaders and forces, so returning colonial powers faced organised movements in 1945.

questions.stem: Which economic effect of the Second World War most weakened Britain's ability to hold its empire?
options: Heavy debts, including to the USA, which made costly colonial wars hard to afford
The loss of all its colonies in Africa to the Axis powers between 1940 and 1945
The collapse of world trade, which left the colonies with nothing worth exporting
A US law that banned Britain from using loan money for any purpose overseas
questions.explanation: Britain ended the war heavily in debt and dependent on American loans, while public opinion favoured spending on reconstruction and the welfare state. India alone needed far more troops to hold than Britain could spare.

questions.stem: Satyagraha, the method Gandhi used against British rule, means:
options: non-violent resistance based on 'truth force'
armed struggle led by a disciplined guerrilla army
negotiation through elected councils only
economic union with Britain and the empire
questions.explanation: Gandhi's satyagraha combined non-violence with mass civil disobedience, boycotts of British goods and non-cooperation with the government. He believed it could change the opponent's heart as well as force concessions.

questions.stem: Independence came through negotiation in Ghana but through prolonged armed struggle in Algeria. Which factor best explains the difference?
options: Algeria had no nationalist party, so violence was the only way to organise resistance
Britain had ruled the Gold Coast for longer, so it was more willing to give it up
Algeria had about a million European settlers and was legally treated as part of France
Ghana's nationalists were better armed than the FLN and frightened Britain into leaving
questions.explanation: Large settler populations, as in Algeria and Kenya, resisted handing power to the majority, and France regarded Algeria's departments as French soil. The Gold Coast had few white settlers, so Britain could transfer power more easily.

questions.stem: How did the Cold War affect decolonisation after 1945?
options: It had no effect, since the USA and USSR stayed out of Asia and Africa entirely
It ended all fighting in the colonies, since the UN banned wars during the Cold War
Superpowers backed rival groups, so some independence struggles became proxy wars
It stopped decolonisation, since both superpowers wanted empires kept unchanged
questions.explanation: Both superpowers opposed old-style empires in principle but competed for influence. The USA sometimes backed colonial powers against movements it feared were communist, and the USSR supported liberation movements, as in Angola.

questions.stem: Angola gained independence in 1975 only after:
options: South Africa invaded Angola and forced Portugal to give up the colony
a military coup in Portugal ended the dictatorship and its colonial wars
the UN sent an army to Angola to expel the Portuguese settlers and troops
Portugal lost a naval war against the newly independent state of Brazil
questions.explanation: Portugal fought costly wars in Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau until the Carnation Revolution of April 1974. Independence was followed by civil war between the MPLA, backed by the USSR and Cuba, and UNITA, backed by the USA and South Africa.

questions.stem: In the Malayan Emergency (1948-1960), Britain fought a mainly communist insurgency yet granted Malaya independence in 1957. What does this suggest about British policy?
options: Britain intended to make Malaya part of the United Kingdom once the insurgency ended
Britain aimed to hand power to friendly non-communist leaders rather than keep direct rule
Britain had been defeated by the insurgents and was forced to leave well before the war ended
Britain wanted to hand Malaya to the Soviet Union to avoid a wider war with China
questions.explanation: Independence under Tunku Abdul Rahman's Alliance undercut the communists' claim to be fighting colonialism. Britain kept ties and bases, a pattern of transferring power to reliable partners seen elsewhere in the Cold War.

questions.stem: During the Suez Crisis of 1956, Britain and France attacked Egypt after Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal. Why is the crisis seen as a sign of the end of empire?
options: The UN handed the canal back to Britain, but France refused to accept it
US pressure forced them to withdraw, showing they could no longer act alone
Egypt's army defeated the British and French forces and captured the whole canal
The USSR occupied the canal zone and held it until the end of the Cold War
questions.explanation: President Eisenhower opposed the invasion and put financial pressure on Britain, which withdrew. The humiliation showed that the old European powers depended on the USA and boosted Nasser and Arab nationalism.

questions.stem: How did the UN Charter of 1945 differ from the League Covenant in its treatment of colonies?
options: It banned colonial powers from joining the UN until they had given up all of their territories
It covered all non-self-governing territories and required powers to report on them
It made all colonies independent immediately and gave them seats in the General Assembly from 1945
It left colonies out entirely, since the Charter dealt only with disputes between sovereign states
questions.explanation: Chapter XI applied to every non-self-governing territory, not just former enemy lands, and Chapters XII and XIII set up the trusteeship system and Trusteeship Council. Britain and France were founding members and permanent Security Council members.

questions.stem: UN General Assembly Resolution 1514 of December 1960 was the:
options: Universal Declaration of Human Rights and its articles on citizenship
treaty that ended the Algerian War and set a vote on independence
Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples
Charter of the Organisation of African Unity and its agreement on fixed borders
questions.explanation: Resolution 1514 declared that subjecting peoples to alien domination denied fundamental human rights and that lack of preparedness should never be a pretext for delaying independence. No state voted against it, though several colonial powers abstained.

questions.stem: Which development best shows the UN moving from supervising colonies to actively pressing for their independence?
options: Adopting the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in December 1948
Setting up a Special Committee in 1961 to monitor how Resolution 1514 was applied
Creating the Trusteeship Council in 1945 to oversee the former League of Nations mandates
Admitting Britain and France as permanent Security Council members in 1945
questions.explanation: The Special Committee on Decolonization, later known as the Committee of 24, examined territories and heard petitioners, keeping pressure on colonial powers. The Trusteeship Council supervised trust territories but did not set out to end colonialism everywhere.

questions.stem: From 1945 Australian waterside workers refused to load Dutch ships bound for Indonesia, and in 1947 Australia took the Dutch-Indonesian conflict to the UN Security Council. What do these actions show?
options: The UN had authorised Australia to send troops to fight alongside Indonesian forces
Britain had asked Australia to help the Netherlands restore its colonial rule there
International pressure, including the UN's, helped force a Dutch transfer of sovereignty
Australia wanted to take over the Dutch East Indies as a UN trust territory of its own
questions.explanation: The Chifley government's appeal led to a UN Good Offices Committee, on which Indonesia chose Australia. Combined with US pressure on the Netherlands, this helped bring the transfer of sovereignty in December 1949.

questions.stem: Muhammad Ali Jinnah's Muslim League passed the Lahore Resolution in 1940. It called for:
options: Muslim support for the British war effort in return for seats in London
independent states in the Muslim-majority areas of north-west and east India
a united India with a Muslim prime minister and a Hindu head of state as well
the return of all of India to rule by the surviving descendants of the Mughals
questions.explanation: The resolution argued that Muslims were a nation and should have autonomous states in Muslim-majority regions. It became the basis of the demand for Pakistan, which Congress opposed.

questions.stem: When Congress launched the Quit India movement in August 1942, the British response was to:
options: invite Gandhi to London to negotiate a new constitution for India in 1943
hand power to the Muslim League and the princes for the rest of the war
arrest Gandhi, Nehru and the Congress leaders and suppress the protests
accept the demand and promise independence as soon as Japan was defeated
questions.explanation: The leaders were jailed within a day and most stayed in prison until 1944-1945, while the Muslim League, which opposed Quit India, strengthened its position. The rising was crushed, but it showed India could not be ruled indefinitely against its will.

questions.stem: Direct Action Day, declared by the Muslim League on 16 August 1946, is remembered for:
options: a peaceful march led by Gandhi to Delhi
the arrest of Jinnah by British troops
the signing of the independence act
mass communal killings in Calcutta
questions.explanation: The League called the day to press its demand for Pakistan, and thousands died in the Great Calcutta Killings. The violence spread and convinced many that partition could not be avoided.

questions.stem: Lord Mountbatten, the last Viceroy, arrived in March 1947. His most controversial decision was to:
options: keep India united under a loose federal constitution against Jinnah's opposition
delay independence until after elections could be held in all the provinces
hand Kashmir to Pakistan before the boundary commission had met at all
bring forward the date of the British withdrawal from June 1948 to August 1947
questions.explanation: Attlee had set June 1948 as the deadline, but Mountbatten moved independence to 15 August 1947. Critics argue the haste left too little time to plan the boundaries and the movement of people, which worsened the violence.

questions.stem: The boundary awards of the Radcliffe Commission were announced on 17 August 1947. Why did this timing contribute to the violence of partition?
options: The British army had already promised to defend the new borders for the next ten years
The awards gave all of Punjab to India and all of Bengal to Pakistan at once
The awards were drawn up by Gandhi and Jinnah, who disagreed on every line
Millions did not know which state they were in until after independence had passed
questions.explanation: Cyril Radcliffe had a few weeks to divide Punjab and Bengal, and the lines were published two days after independence. Communities on the wrong side fled or were attacked, and millions crossed the new borders amid mass killings.

questions.stem: Which problem after independence arose from the princely states, which had been ruled indirectly by Britain?
options: Every princely state declared independence and joined the UN in 1948
The princes all joined Pakistan, cutting India's territory in half
Britain kept the princely states as colonies until the early 1960s
The ruler of Kashmir acceded to India, leading to war with Pakistan in 1947
questions.explanation: Most princely states joined India or Pakistan through the work of Vallabhbhai Patel and V.P. Menon. Hindu ruler Hari Singh of Muslim-majority Kashmir acceded to India in October 1947 as Pakistani tribesmen invaded, beginning a dispute that continues.

questions.stem: Jawaharlal Nehru's main role in India's independence movement was as:
options: commander of the Indian National Army that fought with Japan against Britain
British-appointed governor of Bengal who drew the boundary through Punjab
Congress leader who became India's first prime minister and shaped its secular state
leader of the Muslim League who negotiated the creation of Pakistan with the British
questions.explanation: Nehru, Gandhi's chosen heir, led the interim government from 1946 and was prime minister from 1947 to 1964. Subhas Chandra Bose led the Indian National Army, and Jinnah led the Muslim League.

questions.stem: The Mau Mau uprising in Kenya, which led Britain to declare an emergency in 1952, was rooted mainly in:
options: Kikuyu grievances over land taken for European settlers in the highlands
Somali demands to unite northern Kenya with Italian-ruled Somaliland next door
Indian traders' anger at being refused the vote in colonial elections
a mutiny by Kenyan soldiers returning from service in the Korean War
questions.explanation: Many Kikuyu had lost land in the 'White Highlands' and lived as squatters or in crowded reserves. Britain responded with mass detention camps in which abuse was widespread, as later court cases confirmed.

questions.stem: Jomo Kenyatta was convicted in 1953 of managing Mau Mau and jailed, yet became Kenya's first leader at independence in 1963. What does this best show?
options: Britain had always regarded Kenyatta as loyal and jailed him only to protect him from rebels
The Mau Mau won the war outright and forced Britain to release him in the late 1950s
Kenyans elected him by referendum while he was still in prison under British rule
Britain came to accept nationalist leaders it had jailed as partners in a transfer of power
questions.explanation: Kenyatta's conviction rested on weak evidence. After the Emergency, and scandals such as the Hola camp killings of 1959, Britain moved quickly towards majority rule and dealt with Kenyatta as the leading nationalist.

questions.stem: In May 1945, as Europe celebrated victory, a nationalist march in Setif, Algeria, led to riots and severe French reprisals. Why is this significant?
options: It was the first battle in which the FLN defeated the French army in the open
It led France to give all Algerian Muslims full citizenship and equal votes
It convinced many Algerian nationalists that reform under France was impossible
It ended the Algerian War and led France to grant Algeria independence in that year
questions.explanation: Thousands of Algerians were killed in the reprisals. The FLN's armed rising followed in November 1954, and many of its leaders traced their turn to violence back to Setif.

questions.stem: The crisis over Algeria in May 1958 had which major consequence in France?
options: France abandoned NATO and allied itself with the Soviet Union
The French army withdrew from Algeria within the following month
The settlers declared Algeria an independent white-ruled state
Charles de Gaulle returned to power and founded the Fifth Republic
questions.explanation: Fearing that Paris would negotiate with the FLN, settlers and army officers seized control in Algiers. De Gaulle was recalled, a new constitution followed, and he later moved towards self-determination, which led to independence in 1962.

questions.stem: In 1964 the Organisation of African Unity agreed that member states would respect the borders they had at independence. Why?
options: Redrawing the colonial borders could set off wars across the continent
The borders had been drawn by Africans themselves at the Berlin Conference
The borders matched the ethnic and language groups of every African region
The UN had ruled that colonial borders could never be changed by any state
questions.explanation: Colonial borders cut across peoples and grouped rivals together, but leaders feared that changing them would cause endless conflict. The Berlin Conference of 1884-1885 involved no African states.

questions.stem: Belgian colonial authorities issued identity cards in Rwanda from the 1930s that recorded each person as Hutu, Tutsi or Twa. Which problem of decolonisation does this illustrate?
options: Colonial rule left new states with debts owed to European banks
Colonial rule left no trained officials to run the new government
Colonial rule drew borders that split one people between two states
Colonial rule hardened social categories into rival ethnic identities
questions.explanation: The Belgians favoured the Tutsi minority and fixed identities that had been more fluid, then backed the Hutu majority near independence in 1962. The resulting divisions fed cycles of violence that culminated in the 1994 genocide.

questions.stem: In 1965 Kwame Nkrumah argued that many new states were independent in name but still controlled from outside. This idea, which he called neo-colonialism, refers mainly to:
options: the creation of new empires by African states that conquered their own neighbours
economic dependence on former rulers and foreign companies for trade, aid and investment
the return of European troops to govern the new states directly soon after independence
the rule of new states by settlers from the former colonial power who stayed behind
questions.explanation: Nkrumah's book Neo-Colonialism: The Last Stage of Imperialism argued that economic power, debt and foreign capital allowed former colonial powers and the USA to dominate new states. Many economies depended on exporting one or two raw materials.

questions.stem: Which political problem was common in many newly independent states in the 1960s and 1970s?
options: Former colonial powers formally annexed them again within a decade
Their parliaments were required to include settlers from Europe
They were barred from joining the UN until they held a referendum
Elected governments gave way to one-party rule or military coups
questions.explanation: Leaders often argued that one party was needed for national unity and development; Ghana became a one-party state in 1964 and Nkrumah was overthrown in a coup in 1966. Weak institutions, ethnic division and Cold War interference all played a part.

questions.stem: The Bandung Conference of April 1955 brought together:
options: the colonial powers, meeting to plan a slower pace of independence
the superpowers, meeting to divide Africa into spheres of influence
Commonwealth leaders, meeting to admit India and Pakistan as members
newly independent Asian and African states, hosted by Indonesia
questions.explanation: Twenty-nine Asian and African countries attended, with leaders such as Sukarno, Nehru, Nasser and Zhou Enlai. They condemned colonialism and called for peaceful coexistence, laying groundwork for the Non-Aligned Movement.

questions.stem: The Non-Aligned Movement, founded at Belgrade in 1961 by leaders including Tito, Nehru, Nasser, Sukarno and Nkrumah, aimed to:
options: restore close economic ties with the former colonial powers through the Commonwealth
create a single federal government for Africa and Asia with a capital in Belgrade
keep new states out of the Cold War blocs and give them a stronger collective voice
form a military alliance against the USA under Soviet leadership and protection
questions.explanation: Non-alignment meant refusing to join NATO or the Warsaw Pact. In practice members' relations with the superpowers varied, but the movement gave the developing world a platform in the UN.

questions.stem: UN membership rose from 51 states in 1945 to about 100 by the end of 1960, mostly through decolonisation. Which was the most significant effect on the global balance of power?
options: Newly independent states joined the Warsaw Pact, making the USSR the strongest UN bloc
Newly independent states formed a General Assembly majority that pressed anti-colonial causes
Newly independent states gained vetoes on the Security Council, ending great power control there
Newly independent states gave the USA a permanent two-thirds majority in all UN votes
questions.explanation: With a majority in the General Assembly, new states passed Resolution 1514, condemned apartheid and pushed for economic change, as through the Group of 77 formed in 1964. The Security Council's five permanent members, with their vetoes, did not change.
